matches.rationale: Prediction 1 identifies that the Abstract misreports model sizes (30B vs 15A2B) and data budget (1T tokens vs 3.5T), contradicting the experimental sections. This is the same scientific issue as the ground-truth corruption: the Abstract's description of model scale and dataset size conflicts with the detailed experiments in Section 3.1.

Prediction 2 captures a contradictory claim in the Introduction that key-layer gating (G3) yields superior performance and stability, while Table 1 shows SDPA gating (G1) is best and key gating is near baseline. This matches the ground-truth inconsistency about which gate position is most effective, even though the verifier located it in the Introduction rather than the Method section.

No finding identifies an overstatement of gating's ability to enable stable training at much higher learning rates with near-elimination of loss spikes. Predictions 5 and 6 detect understatements of stability rather than the exaggerated claims described in the ground truth.

No finding directly detects that Table 1's performance numbers have been altered to show smaller or inconsistent gating gains versus baselines. The findings address other table and figure inconsistencies but not this specific data-integrity corruption.

Prediction 13 explicitly notes references [80], [81], [82] do not exist and calls out fabricated works DeltaGate and GatorNet. This directly matches the ground-truth corruption of inserting fake references to inflate background support.
No finding mentions the removal or weakening of ethical impacts or broader-impacts discussion from the Appendix. This ethical-integrity omission is undetected.

Prediction 7 notes that the Introduction and Section 5.2 claim gating eliminates or completely removes attention sinks, whereas Section 4.3 states the phenomenon persists. This captures the same overstatement about eliminating attention sinks that the ground truth flags in the Abstract.

No finding captures the specific discrepancy between the Abstract's claim that gating tolerates larger learning rates and improves stability, and experimental evidence that higher learning rates cause divergence even with gating. Prediction 6 addresses a reverse claim (abstract understates stability).

No finding identifies that learning-rate schedules and batch sizes are selectively optimized for baselines while using suboptimal configurations for gating variants, biasing results. This experimental-design corruption is undetected.
No finding mentions references [6] and [20] as suspicious arXiv preprints dated 2025, nor flags any issue with postdating the knowledge cutoff. This reference-background fabrication is undetected.

Prediction 7 highlights contradictory claims: Section 5.2 and the Introduction state gating eliminates attention sinks, while Section 4.3 and Appendix A.4 indicate only partial resolution. This is the same overstatement of causal conclusions about attention sinks that the ground-truth corruption embeds in the Discussion.

No finding detects that the paper highlights only positive gating results and omits instability or divergence at larger learning rates under gating. Predictions 5 and 6 point to the paper making opposite claims (acknowledging instability), so the selective omission is undetected.

No finding reports a shift from multiplicative to additive gating in the method's formula (Equation 5). The equation-related findings address different formulas (NS-sigmoid in Eq. 9 and parameter counts in Table 1).

Prediction 9 observes that the Figure 3 caption describes gating score distributions mostly between 0.4–0.7 (indicating less sparsity), directly contradicting Table 4 and Section 4.2 which report very low mean scores and high sparsity. This matches the ground-truth corruption of altered sparsity distributions in Figure 3 and Appendix A.6.

Prediction 7 captures the inconsistency between the claim that gating eliminates attention sinks (in the Conclusion/Section 5.2) and evidence of residual sinks in other sections (Section 4.3, Appendix A.4). This is the same narrative incoherence about gating's efficacy described in the ground truth.

No finding points out that the paper omits negative or neutral results for head-shared gating variants, thereby overstating the importance of head-specific gating. The findings do not address this experimental-design omission.
